clinicalPearls: A developmental anomaly in which the crystalline lens is small and abnormally spherical
The increased lens curvature causes marked lenticular myopia
The spherical lens and weak zonules predispose to lens subluxation and to pupillary-block glaucoma
It may be isolated or part of Weill-Marchesani syndrome and other connective tissue disorders
Pupillary block can be paradoxically worsened by miotic drugs and improved by cycloplegics, which is important for management
Careful glaucoma management and lens surgery in selected cases are the mainstays
reference.pathophysiology: Microspherophakia results from arrested lens development leaving a small, highly curved (spherical) lens with attenuated or abnormal zonules. The increased curvature produces high myopia, and the lax zonules allow the lens to move anteriorly. Anterior movement of the spherical lens can obstruct the pupil, causing pupillary-block angle-closure glaucoma; miotics worsen this by relaxing the zonule and allowing further forward lens movement, whereas cycloplegics tighten the zonule and pull the lens back. Zonular weakness also predisposes to frank lens subluxation.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan syndrome and other causes of ectopia lentis
Primary angle-closure glaucoma of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp assessment of lens size, shape and position
Gonioscopy and intraocular pressure for angle-closure risk
Assessment for systemic features of Weill-Marchesani or other syndromes
Family history and genetic evaluation where indicated
redFlags: Systemic features of a connective tissue syndrome
reference.prognosis: With appropriate refractive correction and glaucoma management the prognosis can be reasonable, but recurrent pupillary block and lens dislocation may necessitate surgery and carry risk to vision.
pitfalls: Giving miotics for glaucoma, which worsen pupillary block in spherophakia
Attributing high myopia solely to axial length
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Correct the lenticular myopia with spectacles or contact lenses
Relieve and prevent pupillary-block angle closure with cycloplegic (mydriatic) agents and laser peripheral iridotomy, avoiding miotics which worsen the block
Lower intraocular pressure with topical pressure-lowering agents when glaucoma is present
Undertake lens extraction in selected eyes with recurrent pupillary block or lens subluxation and dislocation
Monitor lifelong for lens subluxation, angle closure and progressive glaucomatous optic nerve damage
Assess for Weill-Marchesani and other connective tissue syndromes, with genetic evaluation and family review
